what_its_for: Gabapentin is used to help control certain types of seizures in people with epilepsy. It is also used to relieve nerve pain (like burning, shooting, or stabbing pain) that can happen after a shingles infection. Some forms are also used for restless leg syndrome. Your doctor may also prescribe it for other conditions not listed here.
how_to_take: Take gabapentin exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food, but taking it with food may help prevent an upset stomach. Swallow capsules and tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or break them unless your doctor says it is okay. If you are taking the liquid form, carefully measure your dose with the special measuring spoon or syringe provided — do not use a regular kitchen spoon. Try to take your doses at the same times every day to keep a steady level of medicine in your body.
dosing: Your dose will be decided by your doctor based on your condition, age, kidney function, and how well you respond to the medicine. Most adults start on a low dose that is slowly increased over time. Doses are often taken 2 to 3 times per day. Do not change your dose on your own — always follow your doctor's instructions. Do not suddenly stop taking gabapentin without talking to your doctor first, as this could cause serious problems like withdrawal or increased seizures.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next scheduled dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store gabapentin at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it out of the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of the reach of children and pets. If you have liquid gabapentin (oral solution), store it in the refrigerator. Do not use medicine that is past its expiration date. Ask your pharmacist how to safely dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking gabapentin, as it can increase dizziness, drowsiness, and the risk of serious side effects. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Be careful when standing up from a sitting or lying position, as gabapentin can cause dizziness and increase your risk of falling. Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of taking gabapentin, as they can make the medicine less effective.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of hurting yourself or suicide, new or worsening depression or anxiety, unusual mood or behavior changes, severe dizziness or trouble breathing, signs of a serious allergic reaction (rash, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, difficulty breathing), muscle weakness, uncontrolled eye movements, or if you feel very sleepy and cannot stay awake. Also call your doctor if your seizures get worse or if you develop swelling in your hands, feet, or legs.
when_it_works: For nerve pain, some people start to feel some relief within 1 to 2 weeks, but it may take 4 to 6 weeks to feel the full benefit. For seizure control, the medicine begins working once you reach the right dose, but it may take several weeks to find that dose. Do not stop taking it just because you do not notice results right away — give it time and keep your follow-up appointments with your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (seniors): You may be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and drowsiness, which increases your risk of falls. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Children: Gabapentin can be used in children for certain types of seizures, but the dose is based on body weight. Watch for behavioral changes, mood swings, or concentration problems in children taking this medicine. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Do not stop taking gabapentin without talking to your doctor first, especially if you take it for seizures. Breastfeeding: Gabapentin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor about the risks and benefits before breastfeeding. Kidney problems: If you have kidney disease or are on dialysis, your dose will need to be adjusted. Always tell your doctor about all your medical conditions and all medicines you are taking.
